theme: Doctrinal Pause: Church Government and Officers
summary: Elders/overseers and deacons, biblical offices, qualifications, and the church’s ordering
readingInstruction: Read 1 Timothy 3:1-13, Titus 1:5-9, and Acts 6:1-6. Today is a doctrinal pause on church government and officers. Notice the qualifications for elders and deacons and how the first servants were appointed.
settingTheScene: How should a church be organized and led? The New Testament does not give a detailed blueprint, but it does describe the roles of elders (also called overseers or pastors) and deacons, and it describes how the early churches appointed them. Christians have drawn different conclusions about the best form of church government, but there is wide agreement about the character and function of the leaders.
observation: “If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task” (1 Timothy 3:1).
“Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain” (1 Timothy 3:8).
“For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 3:13).
“This is why I left you in Crete, so that you might put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town as I directed you” (Titus 1:5).
“He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it” (Titus 1:9).
“Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty” (Acts 6:3).
“But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word” (Acts 6:4).
doctrinalFocus:
The New Testament speaks of two ongoing offices in the local church: elders (presbyteroi), also called overseers (episkopoi) and shepherds or pastors (poimenes), and deacons (diakonoi). Elders lead, teach, and shepherd the flock. Deacons serve, particularly in practical and material needs. The apostles were a unique foundational office, which has not continued.

Elders and overseers appear to be the same office, since Paul uses the terms interchangeably in Titus 1:5-7 and Acts 20:17, 28. Their qualifications emphasize character: above reproach, faithful to their spouse, self-controlled, hospitable, gentle, not greedy, managing their household well. Their tasks are to teach, shepherd, guard the flock from false teaching, and lead. The only ability required is to teach. In Acts 20:28, Paul tells the Ephesian elders to “care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood.”

Deacons came from the appointment of the seven in Acts 6, so that the apostles could devote themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word, while others cared for widows’ food. The seven were “men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom.” Deacons serve the church’s practical needs and free the elders to lead and teach. Romans 16:1 calls Phoebe a deacon (or servant) of the church at Cenchreae. Christians differ on whether women may serve as deacons: some read 1 Timothy 3:11 as referring to women deacons, others to the wives of deacons.

Churches organize themselves in different ways. The episcopal model (Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Methodist) has bishops who oversee multiple congregations. The presbyterian model has elders who govern the church and regional bodies of elders (presbyteries and assemblies). The congregational model (Baptist and many independent churches) holds that the local congregation is the final earthly authority, led by elders and deacons. Disagreements remain over the role of the congregation, the relationship between local churches, and who may hold office, including whether women may be elders. These are important matters, and we should study them in humility.

Agreed principles: leaders are servants, not lords (1 Peter 5:3; Mark 10:42-45). Their authority comes from Scripture. They are accountable to Christ, the chief shepherd, and to the church. The congregation should respect and follow godly leaders (Hebrews 13:17), while testing everything by the word.
interpretation:
1 Timothy 3:1 says that aspiring to the office of overseer is a noble desire. But the emphasis is on character. “Above reproach” means no charge can be brought against his life. “The husband of one wife” is generally understood as faithful to his wife, though Christians differ on whether it excludes divorced and remarried men, singles, or women. “Sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money. He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God’s church? He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit. Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders.” The home is the proving ground.

Deacons likewise must be dignified. They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. They are to be tested first, and then let them serve if they prove themselves blameless. “For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.”

In Titus 1, Paul left Titus in Crete to appoint elders in every town. The qualifications are similar. The elder, as God’s steward, must be above reproach, not arrogant or quick-tempered, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy. “He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it.” The elder both builds up and guards.

Acts 6 shows how the first church solved a problem. The Hellenist widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. The Twelve said, “It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables.” They asked the church to pick out seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and wisdom. The church chose, the apostles prayed and laid hands on them, “and the word of God continued to increase.” Notice the shape: leaders delegate; the congregation participates; the priority is the word and prayer; the result is growth.
connection: Acts 14:23 and 20:17-38 describe the appointment of elders. 1 Peter 5:1-5 gives Peter’s charge to elders. Hebrews 13:7, 17 speak of respecting leaders. Philippians 1:1 greets overseers and deacons. Romans 16:1-2 mentions Phoebe. Ephesians 4:11-12 speaks of shepherds and teachers equipping the saints. 3 John 9-10 warns of a domineering leader. Mark 10:42-45 contrasts Jesus’ model of leadership with the world’s. 1 Corinthians 12:28 lists gifts of administration and helping. Matthew 20:25-28 echoes the servant principle.
application:
Pray for your elders and deacons by name. Thank at least one for something specific.

If God is leading you to aspire to serve as a leader, ask a pastor to help you test it by these qualifications.

Find a practical need in your church and meet it, as the seven did.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus, the Chief Shepherd, for the leaders he has given his church.
Pray for your own church leaders by name.
Ask him to help you follow and support them.
